A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSIvA identifiability study. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments on generalization, identifiability and mixed training in Section 3 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations and controlled experiments in Appendix D.

M1.justification: The CSIvA embeddings, alternating attention, autoregressive adjacency decoder and likelihood objective remain unchanged. Mixed training already appears in v1; v2 expands the data configurations investigated without introducing a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds AutoMPG, Sachs, Sprinkler and Tübingen evaluations, independent-variable pairs with empty graphs, and nonlinear mechanisms sampled from Gaussian processes. These substantially broaden the represented data and task conditions. All reported evaluations remain bivariate.

E2.justification: v1 benchmarks CSIvA against DirectLiNGAM for linear data and NoGAM for nonlinear additive data. v2 retains these comparisons and adds CAM and GraNDAG to broader comparisons against mixed-trained CSIvA on real and simulated datasets (Figures 7–8). These methods were cited but not evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include training on 5,000 and 10,000 datasets alongside the retained 15,000 setting, and training on non-identifiable linear-Gaussian data before testing identifiable models. Real-data evaluation specifies 9 Sachs, 3 AutoMPG, 2 Sprinkler and 102 Tübingen pairs. The original SHD metric and Table 1 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test training-size sensitivity, transfer from non-identifiable training data, discrimination of empty versus connected graphs, and robustness to Gaussian-process mechanism generation (Appendices D.3–D.5 and D.7). The unlimited-budget mixed-training analysis already present in v1 Appendix C is retained as D.6.

E5.justification: Both versions state three training runs and 95% confidence intervals. However, v2's added Figures 6–11 display point estimates without visible intervals or separate uncertainty explanations, unlike v1's experimental figures. This makes reporting less consistent; an increase in repeated runs is not documented.

E6.justification: Figure 1a revises CSIvA's linear-model SHD for Beta and Gumbel noise from approximately 0.15 and 0.17 to near zero, without a stated setting change. Figures 6–11 and 13–16 add substantial benchmark and analysis results. The Gaussian-process results also reveal particularly good PNL generalization across noise distributions.

T1.justification: New Appendix C introduces the formal definition of restricted multivariate additive-noise models, a cited identifiability theorem from Peters et al. and an argument relating these results to transformers. This expands the theoretical scope beyond v1's bivariate analysis. The existing bivariate Proposition 1 and its proof are retained and relocated to Appendix E.

C1.justification: v2 removes the abstract's explicit claim that performance is guaranteed through a formal proof, instead describing theory that explains why ambiguity is rare. It foregrounds OOD failure as a separate contribution. The central claims about training-distribution assumptions and the benefits of mixed training remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning real-data transfer, training-size stability, failure after non-identifiable training and discrimination of independent pairs. Appendix C additionally argues that bivariate findings extend to multivariate models. Appendix D.7 qualifies the noise-shift generalization findings by identifying an exception for Gaussian-process PNL data.

D1.justification: v2 documents Gaussian-process mechanism sampling using a zero-mean process with a unit-bandwidth RBF kernel and explains extraction of bivariate benchmark pairs without introducing new confounding. The original architecture details, hyperparameters, hardware, runtime figures and causally-library access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against Lopez-Paz et al., distinguishing their learning-rate results under assumed identifiability, and discusses Dai et al.'s skeleton-learning work. Appendices B.2 and D.7 broaden the data-generation literature review. The existing identifiability proposition is also repositioned as a corollary rather than an extension of earlier results.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and identifiability explanation receive targeted rewrites. Related work becomes a separate section, Proposition 1 moves into the appendix, and supplementary experiments receive subsections. Much of the existing method description, experimental narrative and proof text remains closely aligned.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with benchmark, sensitivity, independence and Gaussian-process result figures. The original Figure 6 becomes Figure 12 rather than disappearing. Figures 2–3 receive corrected panel descriptions, and the document adopts a different title, author and heading layout.

improvement.justification: The added benchmark evaluations, Gaussian-process replications and controlled analyses strengthen the mixed-training evidence beyond v1's narrower synthetic study. Caption corrections and clearer attribution also help. The net gain is limited by missing uncertainty displays in new Figures 6–11, broad benchmark-dominance language despite exceptions in Figures 7–8, and Appendix C's extrapolation from bivariate experiments without establishing multivariate transformer performance.
